issues.issue: The operative date is handwritten and garbled — "Aust { i 997" — so the effective date cannot be read off the instrument with confidence. A mechanical defect of this kind directly changes when the Agreement took effect.

The stated 1997 effective date cannot be reconciled with the preamble, which recites that the Agreement is made in 1999. A court asked when the custodial duties began would have to choose between them.

The Custodian is given a bare election — segregated holding "or" fungible bulk under a FOSBI arrangement — with no criteria and no notice obligation, and FOSBI is not defined. Which branch applies to any given security is not fixed by the text.
The clause permits four alternative registrations without saying who elects among them or on what basis. The permissive string leaves the Owner's protection dependent on an unallocated choice.

Registration "in the name of the Custodian or its nominee" sits in tension with Section 13, which requires the Custodian's records to identify the securities as "owned by the Owner", and with Section 15's withdrawal-on-demand right. The relationship of legal title to those rights is not spelled out.

"[T]o the extent required by those sections" makes the Commissioner's control depend on external statutes without identifying which securities are so "used to meet the deposit requirements". The boundary of the exception must be worked out from outside the document.

The absolute statement that custodied securities are "withdrawable upon the demand of the Owner" conflicts with Section 6(c)/(d), under which delivery on termination is subject to the Custodian's right to withhold for outstanding fees and balances. Both are stated in unqualified terms.

"[A]t such times and containing such information as may be reasonably requested" leaves the content and frequency of reporting entirely to an unbounded reasonableness standard. What a request may compel is not fixed.

This duplicates and overlaps Section 3's reporting obligations without saying which governs where they differ, leaving two reporting regimes in one instrument. The overlap is redundant rather than plainly contradictory.

"[A]ny representative of an appropriate regulatory body" and "an appropriate officer of the Owner" both turn on an undefined "appropriate", which decides who may compel access. The gatekeeping condition is therefore not self-applying.

The "but only upon furnishing ... written instructions" precondition cannot be squared with Section 9, which subjects the Custodian's books, records and practices to examination by the Owner with no conditions at all. A court would have to decide whether Section 17 qualifies Section 9.

The trailing qualifier "that the Owner may reasonably request" is ambiguous as to whether it limits only clause (b) or both (a) and (b), which decides whether clearing-corporation reports must be sent automatically. The syntax alone will not resolve it.

"[R]ecords sufficient to determine and verify information ... that may be reported in the Owner's Annual Statement" sets no ascertainable standard of sufficiency. What suffices is judged only after the fact.

"[M]ysterious disappearance" is a term of art with contested boundaries, and the clause mixes fault-based triggers (negligence, dishonesty) with no-fault ones (theft, mysterious disappearance, damage or destruction), so the standard of liability is not settled by the words. "[L]oss of custodied securities" is likewise undefined as against loss of value.

This liability cannot readily be reconciled with Section 7, under which the Owner indemnifies the Custodian for all claims incurred by acting as Custodian except where the Custodian was negligent or committed malfeasance — leaving no-fault losses indemnified in both directions. Section 23's force-majeure exculpation pulls the same way.

"[S]hall promptly replace the securities or the value thereof" does not say who elects between replacement in kind and payment, or as of what date value is fixed, and "the value of any loss of rights or privileges" is unquantified. The remedy is left unspecified in a clause whose whole purpose is remedy.

The exculpation ends in a catch-all — "or similar causes beyond its reasonable control" — appended to a long list of specific events, so ejusdem generis leaves its reach genuinely open; the list also contains the mechanical error "lot" for "riot". Whether an event is "similar" to war, strikes and acts of God is precisely what parties would dispute.

A blanket exculpation for "any failure to take any action required to be taken under the Agreement" is hard to reconcile with Section 21, which makes the Custodian liable for no-fault losses including theft and mysterious disappearance. A court would have to decide whether Section 23 cuts down Section 21.

The proviso lets "the Insurance Commissioner of the state of domicile of the insurance company" accept a different standard of liability, but the Agreement never defines "the insurance company" and gives no mechanism or timing for that acceptance. The clause's operation is left to an outside actor on undefined terms.

"[I]nsurance protection consistent with the requirements of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency" incorporates an unidentified external standard and fixes no amount, coverage or duration. Whether the warranty was met cannot be judged from the words alone.
